primary_cause: Macro/retail recession repricing rather than a Lowe's-specific event. No clear Lowe's-specific negative headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: General de-risking in cyclical retail and concern that store traffic and big-ticket discretionary purchases would weaken sharply during lockdowns
store_description: No discrete Lowe's corporate headline convincingly explains a 4.8% one-day move. The best explanation is that investors were discounting a severe COVID shutdown hit to U.S. consumer spending and upcoming earnings.

primary_cause: Cyclical semiconductor equipment de-rating on worsening global demand expectations. No Lam-specific Reuters negative in the 3-day window
secondary_factors: General tech profit-taking after the sharp rebound from March lows and concern over memory/fab spending if the recession deepened
store_description: No strong company-specific Lam catalyst visible in the window so the most likely explanation is a sector move tied to fears that the COVID shock would hit wafer-fab equipment demand and customer capex.

primary_cause: COVID-driven collapse in spending especially travel-related and cross-border payments volumes. No Mastercard-only headline in the immediate window
secondary_factors: Financial-sector weakness after big-bank results reinforced how severe the shutdown shock was likely to be
store_description: No Mastercard-only headline but the business was directly exposed to the areas being hit hardest by lockdowns including travel entertainment and cross-border payments. The 5.0% drop is most plausibly a repricing of transaction-volume risk.

primary_cause: Restaurant traffic and operating disruption from COVID lockdowns. No McDonald's-specific Reuters headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Investors rotating out of consumer-facing defensives into names with more visible earnings resilience
store_description: No discrete April 12-15 McDonald's announcement stands out as the trigger. The most likely cause is a straightforward repricing of shutdown-driven sales pressure with dining rooms closed or restricted across many markets.

primary_cause: Elective-procedure shutdowns hurting medical-device demand. No new MDT-specific headline in the 3-day window
secondary_factors: Broader de-risking in healthcare names without near-term COVID testing/treatment upside
store_description: Medtronic's core businesses depended heavily on procedures that hospitals were delaying to preserve capacity for COVID patients. The 3.8% decline is most consistent with investors further marking down near-term procedure volumes and hospital purchasing activity.

primary_cause: Industrial recession fears outweighing PPE demand enthusiasm. No decisive 3M-specific negative headline during April 12-15
secondary_factors: Concerns that non-healthcare segments would weaken sharply as manufacturing and commercial activity slowed
store_description: Even though N95 demand was booming 3M was still a broad industrial company with meaningful exposure to a collapsing global economy. The 3.3% drop looks like investors deciding that earnings damage across industrial and transportation end markets would dominate respirator sales.

primary_cause: Earnings-driven reset from COVID credit costs plus payment-services exposure to travel/retail. U.S. Bancorp reported Q1 EPS of $0.72 and said results were adversely impacted by COVID-19
secondary_factors: Sympathy pressure from JPMorgan/Wells Fargo results that had already framed a grim bank outlook
store_description: USB's selloff is one of the clearer ones with the bank reporting $0.72 EPS and saying the quarter was hurt by COVID. Its disclosed revenue mix showed material exposure to travel at 12% and retail at 28% which were exactly the categories being frozen by lockdowns.

primary_cause: Commercial-aerospace demand collapse after the RTX merger closed. The combined company had major commercial-aerospace exposure just as global air travel collapsed
secondary_factors: Integration uncertainty and broad aerospace selloff as airlines grounded fleets
store_description: The new RTX entity came into existence only days earlier inheriting sizable exposure to Pratt & Whitney and other aerospace businesses just as airlines worldwide were grounding aircraft making the stock highly sensitive to the ongoing air-travel collapse.

primary_cause: Earnings day reaction to weaker profitability and integration-related expenses. Charles Schwab reported Q1 net income of $795 million down 18% year over year
secondary_factors: Lower rates pressuring net interest revenue and broader financial-sector weakness after bank earnings
store_description: This looks primarily earnings-driven with Schwab saying first-quarter net income fell to $795 million from $964 million a year earlier while absorbing transaction/integration costs giving investors a reason to mark down earnings power despite elevated client activity.

primary_cause: Macro-driven utility selloff amid recession and demand concerns. No Southern Company-specific negative headline in the window
secondary_factors: Rotation and balance-sheet sensitivity fears in rate-sensitive sectors
store_description: No strong Southern-specific event in the 3 days before the drop. The 5.3% decline looks mostly like a macro move with utilities sold alongside other defensives as markets digested worsening shutdown economics and earnings uncertainty.

primary_cause: COVID pressure on media/advertising and general leveraged-defensive repricing. No AT&T-specific April 12-15 Reuters headline
secondary_factors: Broad market concern over recession hitting wireless upgrades advertising and entertainment distribution
store_description: No single AT&T headline causing the move. The most plausible explanation is investors discounting weaker WarnerMedia and ad revenue plus a tougher environment for a highly leveraged telecom-media hybrid during the lockdown shock.

primary_cause: Anticipation of weak enterprise IT/services demand and services revenue pressure. IBM's later results showed revenue of $17.6 billion down 3.4%
secondary_factors: Rotation out of slower-growth legacy tech/services names during a recession scare
store_description: No discrete IBM headline in April 12-15 but the later April 20 print validated what investors were already worried about with legacy services and infrastructure demand weakening under COVID and quarterly revenue down 3.4%.

primary_cause: Collapse in consumer and especially cross-border card spending. No stronger Visa-specific event in the 3-day window
secondary_factors: Sympathy weakness with Mastercard and broader financials
store_description: Visa's business mix made it highly exposed to travel and international commerce both of which were freezing in mid-April 2020. The 5.0% drop is best explained as a reassessment of payment-volume and cross-border fee pressure.

primary_cause: Earnings-driven selloff from massive reserve build and worsening credit outlook. Wells Fargo reported Q1 results on April 14 with profit plunging as the bank built huge loan-loss reserves
secondary_factors: Spillover from JPMorgan and broader bank-sector repricing
store_description: This was a classic earnings/credit-cost reaction with Wells April 14 results showing the bank taking a large hit from expected loan losses just as peers signaled the same. The market interpreted that as confirmation that shutdown-related defaults and reserve builds would be far worse.

primary_cause: IEA demand-shock forecast crushing confidence in oil fundamentals. On April 15 the IEA said global oil demand in 2020 would fall by 9.3 million bpd and April demand alone could be down roughly 29 million bpd
secondary_factors: Storage-capacity fears and skepticism that OPEC+ cuts were enough
store_description: Exxon's 4.6% fall lines up very closely with the IEA's April 15 oil-market report projecting a 9.3 million bpd demand decline for 2020 and an unprecedented 29 million bpd collapse for April. For an integrated oil major that was a direct negative on upstream prices and cash flow.

primary_cause: Bank/financial-sector de-rating ahead of earnings after peers exposed the scale of the COVID credit shock. Morgan Stanley later reported net revenues of $9.5 billion down from $10.3 billion
secondary_factors: Concern about investment-banking and wealth activity amid market turmoil
store_description: MS had not yet reported on April 15 so the most likely trigger was the market extrapolating from JPMorgan and Wells to the rest of the group. That proved directionally reasonable as Morgan Stanley's next-day results showed revenue down.

primary_cause: Aerospace-end-market deterioration. No Honeywell-specific headline in the 3-day window but the company's large aerospace exposure was becoming a major problem
secondary_factors: Broader industrial recession worries
store_description: The absence of a fresh company headline suggests the move was more about investors repricing aerospace suppliers as airline demand collapsed. Honeywell's later decision to pull guidance on weak aero demand fits that interpretation.

primary_cause: GE Aviation exposure to the collapse in global air travel. No GE-specific April 12-15 Reuters headline but aviation exposure made it one of the most vulnerable large industrials
secondary_factors: Balance-sheet concerns and general industrial recession risk
store_description: GE's 6.2% drop is best explained by its extreme sensitivity to commercial aerospace where engine demand maintenance activity and airline capital spending were all being crushed. This looks like continued repricing of aviation-driven earnings and cash-flow risk.

primary_cause: Auto-demand collapse plus shutdown-related production and liquidity stress. The company remained under heavy pressure from plant shutdowns and cash-burn fears
secondary_factors: Supplier-chain disruption and recession fears
store_description: GM's decline fits the broader auto shutdown narrative with factories idled dealerships disrupted and investors focused on how much cash automakers would burn before reopening. 2020 volumes and profitability were going to be much worse than previously expected.

primary_cause: Expected slowdown in consulting/project spend as clients delayed discretionary work. No fresh Accenture-specific negative on April 12-15
secondary_factors: Rotation out of economically sensitive services names
store_description: No obvious Accenture-only headline in the window so the cleanest explanation is a macro-driven reset in consulting demand expectations with investors increasingly assuming clients would defer transformation and advisory work.
